messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin had spent three decades building a career around his eye for space and beauty — the way light moved through a room, the way a carefully chosen palette could make a client feel at home in their own life. At fifty-seven, he was respected, unhurried, and largely content. That changed on a Tuesday afternoon in March, when he was driving back from a client consultation in his familiar silver sedan and a delivery truck ran a red light at approximately forty miles an hour, striking the driver's side with a force that folded the door inward and spun the car across two lanes of traffic. Martin was conscious throughout. He heard the shriek of metal before he understood what was happening, felt the impact travel through his left side like something geological, and then sat trapped in the wreckage for twenty-two minutes while traffic stopped around him and strangers pressed their faces to the shattered window. He was certain, in those twenty-two minutes, that he was dying.

He was not. He sustained a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, and a concussion, and was discharged from the hospital after four days. Physically, his recovery proceeded more or less as the doctors had predicted. Psychologically, it did not.

In the weeks following the accident, Martin began noticing that certain things undid him entirely. The sound of a car braking hard on the street outside his apartment — the low, compressed squeal of tires — would stop him mid-sentence, mid-breath, mid-thought. His heart would accelerate before his mind had even registered what it had heard. When he drove past an intersection where two cars had been pulled to the shoulder after a minor fender-bender, the sight of the crumpled panels and the angle of one vehicle against the other sent him into a state he could not easily name or exit. Colleagues occasionally mentioned road accidents in passing — a client delayed by a pile-up, a news story about highway fatalities — and Martin found himself excusing himself from those conversations with an abruptness that he later felt embarrassed by, though not embarrassed enough to stay.

His work, which had always required him to drive between client sites across the city, became the specific terrain in which these responses were most relentless. He could not pull into a parking structure without scanning every moving vehicle as a potential projectile. He could not sit in traffic without monitoring the rearview mirror with a vigilance that left him exhausted by the time he arrived anywhere. Over several months, he began scheduling fewer site visits, delegating more to his junior associate, and conducting as much business as possible by video call. Clients noticed. One long-standing relationship ended quietly when Martin declined, for the third time, to visit a renovation in progress.

What troubled him most, though, was not the fear itself but what he had come to believe it meant. He had always thought of his body as something fundamentally reliable — a tool he neither pampered nor doubted. Now he was certain that this was no longer true, that the accident had revealed some fragility that had always been present but was now exposed and permanent. He had been damaged in a way that could not be undone, and he was certain of this not as a fear but as a fact. Stranger still was the sense that he no longer recognised himself in any reliable way — the man who had moved through the world with quiet confidence felt like someone he was reading about rather than inhabiting. He did not know who he was now, and that disorientation sat beneath everything else like a low, continuous pressure.

He came to therapy at the suggestion of his physician, who had noted his elevated heart rate and sleep disturbance at a routine follow-up. Martin arrived composed and articulate, describing his symptoms with the precision of someone who had been observing himself carefully. What he said he most wanted was to be able to drive to a client's home without spending the journey in a state of controlled dread. What he feared, though he said it quietly and only once, was that the person capable of doing that no longer existed.
